title: Living in the world
hook: asked how to get through the world, Nanak points to a lotus and a duck in the water

segments.voice: Yesterday the yogis asked the guest who he was, and Nanak answered with a seat in every heart. Your line was who are you. Did you find your one line? Today the next question. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-four.

A duck spends its whole day in the pond. It dives for food, paddles against the current, gets splashed by every other duck. Then it climbs out onto the bank, gives one shake, and the water simply isn't there anymore. The feathers underneath are dry. That small animal is the answer to a serious question in the Sidh Gosht. A yogi named Charpat puts it to Nanak: the world is an ocean, hard to cross, they say. So how does anyone get to the other side? Today: living in the world, and why the answer swims.
screen: `IN THE POND ALL DAY.` → `ONE SHAKE, AND DRY.` → `CHARPAT: HOW DO WE CROSS?`

segments.voice: Nanak's reply, in paraphrase: as the lotus stays apart in the water, and as the duck swims in the stream and stays dry, so a person can live. Earlier on this path we stayed with the lotus, the flower that rises clean out of the mud. Today, look at the duck, because it's doing something the lotus isn't. A lotus is rooted. It stays in one place and lets the water move around it. A duck goes places. It hunts, it feeds its young, it fights the current, it's busy all day. Of the two pictures, the duck is the one with a job. That matters, because the yogis in this poem had answered the world by leaving the household behind, going where the water can't reach. Nanak doesn't tell them they're wrong to love stillness. He just points at a bird that is completely in the water and comes out dry. You don't have to leave the stream to stay untouched by it. The same stanza adds another phrase: living with hopes all around and not being ruled by them, keeping the One settled in the mind. That's the duck's secret said without the bird. The hopes, the worries, the deadlines are real water. They just don't get under the feathers. And this is where the week has been heading. It began with the last of the ragas, many moods and one Word. Then a circle sat down on the mountain, and the first question was who are you. Today's answer gives that self somewhere to live: not a cave, not a peak, but the stream, swimming. In Sikh teaching that picture belongs to the householder, the person with work, a family and bills, who keeps the Name in mind through all of it. The duck stays dry.
screen: `THE LOTUS STAYS. THE DUCK SWIMS.` · `NO NEED TO LEAVE THE STREAM.` · `HOPES ALL AROUND, NOT RULED BY THEM.` · `THE HOUSEHOLDER'S PICTURE.` · then, large: `THE DUCK STAYS DRY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay calm in one busy moment. Start by rehearsing it here. Bring to mind the busiest stretch waiting for you today: the commute, the inbox, the kitchen at dinnertime. Picture yourself right in it, moving and working, not watching from the side. Now picture the duck, paddling hard, and the water rolling off its back. Breathe in: in the stream. Breathe out: dry underneath. Stay with that for a few rounds. Later, when that moment arrives for real, give it one breath and one shake. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each slow breath. The bell holds the time.
Living in the world. Nanak's answer to Charpat: like the lotus apart in the water, like the duck that swims the stream and stays dry. Today's word.
Your line: the duck stays dry. In the busiest moment today, keep swimming, then give one small shake of the shoulders and let what isn't yours roll off. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of this stanza when describing the householder's life, grihasti: working, raising a family and serving others while keeping the Name in mind, rather than withdrawing from the world.

myth: in Nanak's picture, the duck leaves the water to stay dry
it swims in the stream and stays dry; it never leaves the water.
the question behind the picture is how to cross the world-ocean
Charpat asks how anyone gets across the world, an ocean hard to cross.

he doesn't attack their stillness; he points to a bird that is fully in the water and stays dry.

fork.setup: you're a yogi who believes the only way to stay pure is to leave the world. you ask Nanak how to get across. what does he point to?
options: a cave high on the mountain.
a duck swimming in the stream.
a boat that never touches water.
fork.reveal: he points to the lotus and the duck: fully in the water, and untouched by it.

original.note: murgaaee: the water bird in the stanza, swimming in the stream and staying dry.

trapdoor: what you thought: to stay pure, you have to get out of the water.
what it means: Nanak's duck swims all day in the stream and comes out dry.
what a scholar hears: the lotus and the duck answer a renunciate's question with the householder's ideal, set in the yogis' own image of the world-ocean.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ramkali, Mahala 1, Sidh Gosht, pauris 4–5, Ang 938 (Charpat's question; the lotus and the duck)

notes: Pauri 5 paraphrased: Charpat asks how to cross the world-ocean, called hard to cross; Nanak answers with the lotus apart in water and the duck swimming in the stream, and adds living amid hopes without hope (aasaa maahi niraaso) with the One in mind. The stanza's 'surat sabad' crossing line is held back for day 1140. Please confirm the attribution to Charpat and the paraphrase.
The contrast between the rooted lotus and the working duck is the script's own reflection, not a claim about the text; please confirm it is fair.
